title: NEXORA FailurePolicy
description: The three distinct failure planes (docs/architecture/30-failure-policy.md). Fail-closed is the default; the block mechanism is a FixedProfile aimed at a CLOSED loopback port, because '+direct' and chrome.proxy.settings.clear() both leak traffic. Schema enforces the one thing that must never be true: no connector-failure path may resolve to DIRECT or SYSTEM -- which is why coreDeath.action and serviceTeardown.then are single-value enums here, why the allOf at the bottom refuses a narrowed forbiddenOutcomes, and why failOpen survives only in $defs/ProfilePolicy under a required confirmToken.

version.description: Document version of the global policy, migrated independently of -nexora.schemaVersion (docs/architecture/35-schema-versioning-migration.md §4).

coreDeath.description: The Xray process exited or stopped responding while the Connector is alive. Highest-severity plane: traffic is still being routed somewhere.

action.description: The global plane has exactly one resolution: block. ADR-0009 rule 2 forbids a global fail-open -- 'a product whose default is fail-open has no failure policy' -- so 'failOpen' lives only in #/$defs/ProfilePolicy, where the if/then there makes the user's confirmToken required. Spelled as a single-value enum rather than a const so that a rejecting validator reports the allowed set instead of a value mismatch.

notify.description: Gates the restart-ladder noise, not the verdict. The terminal blocked state is surfaced whatever this says: ADR-0009 rule 7, and settings.proxy.notificationLevel cannot be 'silent' for a block (docs/architecture/30-failure-policy.md section 4).

serviceTeardown.description: The Connector process itself is gone (host shim disconnected, machine sleep, upgrade). Different from coreDeath because the Connector may come back and re-apply the same config.

graceSeconds.description: Keep the current chrome.proxy setting while the Connector may come back. This is the only case where leaving the proxy in place is correct, and it is bounded by hardCapSeconds.

then.description: Not 'restore'. A Connector-triggered resolution that hands the browser back its pre-NEXORA setting ends at direct or system egress, which forbiddenOutcomes forbids; 'restore' therefore exists only under extensionLifecycle, where the trigger is the user removing the extension rather than a Connector failing. The field stays an enum of one because the alternative has to remain visible in the contract, not hidden in prose.

extensionLifecycle.description: Events driven by the browser, not by the Connector. Must never depend on the Connector being reachable (docs/audit/06).

onBrowserStart.description: 'reapply' is today's startupCheck behaviour and must not regress (docs/audit/06).

block.description: The fail-closed primitive: a chrome.proxy FixedProfile aimed at a port nothing listens on. Chosen over '+direct' and proxy.settings.clear() because both of those leak traffic instead of stopping it (ADR-0009).

forbiddenOutcomes.description: Machine-checkable statement of 'no silent proxy bypass'. scripts/verify.mjs asserts these never appear as a connector-failure resolution, and verification row LIVE-11 asserts it at runtime.

action.description: Per-profile override. 'failOpen' here does not weaken the global default for other profiles.

confirmToken.description: Evidence that the user explicitly accepted fail-open for this profile. Required whenever action is failOpen, by the if/then below, so that no implementation can silently weaken ADR-0009 and a validator in any language rejects the same document.

allOf.description: ADR-0009 rule 5 is a prohibition, not a preference. minItems alone would let a document name one forbidden outcome and permit the other two, so the set is pinned element by element: a policy that writes forbiddenOutcomes at all must forbid all three. Omitting the key stays legal, because the default is the full set -- which is why these are properties branches rather than required ones.

'system' is the legacy SystemProfile gesture: chrome.proxy.settings.clear() hands the decision to whatever the OS or an enterprise policy says (docs/audit/06-proxy-application.md section 4), which is the same leak wearing a management name.

clear() as an outcome is forbidden for the same reason. Note that extensionLifecycle.onDisabled = 'restore' is not the same act: there the user removed the extension, the browser plane is not responding to a Connector failure, and the prohibition in this array is scoped to connector-triggered resolutions.
